chunks: Yahya al-Halabi, from Abdullah ibn Muskan, from Habeeb who said:

I heard Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) saying: 'By Allah, there is no one from the people more beloved to me than you. Indeed, people have taken various paths; among them is one who took his own opinion, among them is one who followed his desires, and among them is one who followed narration. But you have taken hold of a matter that has an origin. So upon you is piety and independent reasoning, and to witness the funerals, and to visit the sick, and to be present with your people in their mosques for prayer. Is it not shameful for a man among you that his neighbor knows his right while he does not know the right of his neighbor?'
ai.seo_question: What are the key practices recommended for Shia Muslims to distinguish themselves and maintain social bonds according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: In this hadith from al-Kafi, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) distinguishes his followers from the general populace by highlighting their adherence to a tradition with a solid foundation (asl), contrasting them with those driven by personal opinion, desire, or mere narration. He emphasizes the necessity of wara' (piety/conscientiousness) and ijtihad (independent reasoning) as essential practices for maintaining this distinct identity. The narration further underscores the social dimension of faith, urging active participation in communal rituals like funerals and congregational prayers, while critiquing the neglect of neighborly rights as a failure of self-accounting.

en.hubeali: H 14569 – Yahya Al-Halby, from Abdullah Bin Muskaan, from Habeeb who said:

I heard Abu Abdullahasws saying: ‘By Allahazwj! There is no one from the people more beloved to measws than you are, and that the people have gone in various directions. So among them is the ‘one’ who takes (religion) to his own opinion, and among them is one who follows his own desires, and among them is the one who follows the narration (Al-Riwayah), and you all have grabbed to a matter for which there is an origin. So it is for you to observe piety, and the struggle, and bear witness to the funerals, and console the sick, and be present with your people in their Masjids for the Prayers. Is it not shameful for the man among you that his right is being observed by his neighbour whilst he himself does not observe the rights of his neighbour?’
